query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability is primarily governed by the configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch, which together favor the formation of a single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution over intermetallic compounds. This stabilization mechanism enables the retention of desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness by suppressing brittle intermetallic phases and promoting a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy, equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition, homogenized and solution-treated.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of Al content while keeping other elements constant, to tune the atomic size mismatch and electron concentration.
generation.conditions: Samples annealed at 1000°C for 24 hours followed by water quenching; mechanical and environmental tests performed at room temperature, 77 K (cryogenic), and 800°C (high temperature).
generation.structural_mediator: Phase constitution (single-phase FCC, BCC, or multiphase with intermetallics) and microstructural homogeneity.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy and moderate atomic size mismatch stabilize solid solution phases by reducing the Gibbs free energy, suppressing the formation of ordered intermetallics that would otherwise degrade mechanical and environmental properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with moderate Al content (e.g., 0.5–1.5 at. ratio) will retain a single-phase solid solution (FCC or BCC) with superior combinations of high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness compared to alloys with higher Al content, which will form brittle intermetallics and exhibit degraded properties.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy exhibiting a single-phase FCC or BCC structure with balanced properties.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with total atomic size mismatch below ~6% and configurational entropy above 1.5R; outside these ranges, intermetallics may form and degrade properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of Al content and atomic size mismatch for phase transition may vary with processing history and minor impurities; the role of short-range order is not fully addressed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with varying Al content (e.g., 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 atomic ratios), anneal under identical conditions, and characterize phase constitution (XRD, SEM-EDS), mechanical properties (tensile, fracture toughness at room and cryogenic temperatures), oxidation resistance (TGA at 800°C), and radiation tolerance (ion irradiation, TEM).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with high atomic size mismatch and/or low configurational entropy (e.g., high Al content) retain a single-phase solid solution and exhibit comparable or superior property combinations to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
